name: Change that destroys skills
idea: The work argues that technology advances step by step until broken by discontinuities, which either enhance or destroy the competence of existing firms. Competence-destroying change, it argues, tends to come from new entrants and to make the market more turbulent, while competence-enhancing change tends to come from existing firms and to make it less so.
suggests: Look at whether a new technology in a market builds on what existing firms already know how to do, or makes that knowledge obsolete.
limits: The work argues that such discontinuities are rare and arrive at irregular intervals, so long periods of step-by-step change lie between them.
competing_idea: Another view holds that even changes that leave a product's components much the same can defeat established firms, when they alter how the components are linked.
questions: Does this new technology build on the existing firms' skills, or make them obsolete?
Who is bringing it to market: established firms or new entrants?
Has the market become more turbulent since it appeared, with firms entering, leaving or changing places?

originals.reference: Michael L. Tushman and Philip Anderson, "Technological Discontinuities and Organizational Environments", Administrative Science Quarterly, Vol. 31 No. 3, September 1986, pp. 439-465

Rebecca M. Henderson and Kim B. Clark, "Architectural Innovation: The Reconfiguration of Existing Product Technologies and the Failure of Established Firms", Administrative Science Quarterly, Vol. 35 No. 1, March 1990, pp. 9-30
